## Governing Equations

### 1 · Gurney: Initial Fragment Velocity

For a cylindrical shell the Gurney formula gives initial fragment velocity $V_0$:

$$
V_0 = \sqrt{2E} \left(\frac{M}{C} + \tfrac{1}{2}\right)^{-1/2} \quad (1)
$$

| Symbol      | Description                                  | Unit |
| ----------- | -------------------------------------------- | ---- |
| $\sqrt{2E}$ | Gurney energy constant (explosive-dependent) | m/s  |
| $M$         | Metal (shell body) mass                      | kg   |
| $C$         | Explosive filler mass                        | kg   |
| $V_0$       | Initial fragment velocity                    | m/s  |

Gurney constants: 2 440 m/s (TNT), 2 700 m/s (Comp-B), 2 930 m/s (RDX).

### 2 · Shell State at Break-up

The shell expands under detonation pressure before fracturing. Pearson (1990) and
the PAFRAG methodology set break-up at approximately three times the initial internal
volume of explosive products (V/V₀ ≈ 3). For a cylindrical geometry the inner
radius grows as:

$$
r_{i,\text{bu}} = r_{i,0}\,\sqrt{3} \quad (2a)
$$

Assuming the steel wall is incompressible (volume conserved during radial expansion):

$$
r_{o,\text{bu}} = \sqrt{r_{i,\text{bu}}^2 + (r_{o,0}^2 - r_{i,0}^2)} \quad (2b)
$$

The Mott formula uses the **mean** shell radius at break-up:

$$
r_{\text{bu}} = \tfrac{1}{2}(r_{i,\text{bu}} + r_{o,\text{bu}}) \quad (2c)
$$

| Symbol                                  | Description                   | Unit |
| --------------------------------------- | ----------------------------- | ---- |
| $r_{i,0}$, $r_{o,0}$                   | Initial inner/outer radii     | m    |
| $r_{i,\text{bu}}$, $r_{o,\text{bu}}$ | Inner/outer radii at break-up | m    |
| $r_{\text{bu}}$                        | Mean shell radius at break-up | m    |

**Case velocity at break-up (eq. 2d).** Eq. (1) is the *terminal* velocity —
the whole Gurney energy delivered at infinite expansion. The case is still
accelerating when it fractures at $\eta_{\text{bu}} = V/V_{\text{charge}} \approx
3$, so the fracture chain of §3 must be evaluated at the smaller
break-up-instant speed $v_{\text{bu}} = f V_0$. Applying the same partition at
finite $\eta$ makes the $(M/C + \tfrac12)$ factor cancel in the ratio, leaving
the released-energy fraction alone; with $pV^{\gamma_g} = \text{const}$ from the
CJ state,

$$
f = \frac{v_{\text{bu}}}{V_0}
  = \sqrt{1 - \eta_{\text{bu}}^{-(\gamma_g - 1)}} \quad (2d)
$$

| Symbol                | Description                                       | Unit |
| --------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- | ---- |
| $\eta_{\text{bu}}$   | Gas-cavity volume expansion ratio at break-up     | —    |
| $\gamma_g$            | Detonation-product isentrope (gas) exponent       | —    |
| $f$                   | Case-speed fraction $v_{\text{bu}}/V_0$ at break-up | —  |
| $v_{\text{bu}}$      | Case speed at break-up                            | m/s  |

$\gamma_g$ (a *gas* isentrope exponent, ~3) is not Mott's fracture constant
$\gamma'$ (~55) of §3 — the two are ~20× apart and must not be confused. $f$ is
`breakup_velocity_fraction()` and is printed in §5; the honest band is
0.90–0.95, taken from a $\gamma_g$ sweep against a completion-ratio variant.
$f$ enters **only** the fracture chain: the fragment *launch* velocity used by
the drag, energy, and lethality sections stays the terminal $V_0$ of eq. (1)
(two instants, one model). Derivation, bracket checks against Kennedy's grazing
data, and the $\eta$ bookkeeping across the registry:
`updates/breakup-velocity-fraction/derivation.md`.

### 3 · Mott: Fragment Mass Distribution

At break-up, stress-release waves arrest further fracture in their wake (Mott 1947).
The cumulative fragment count is:

$$
N(m) = N_0 \, \exp\!\left(-\sqrt{m / \mu}\right) \quad (3)
$$

where $N_0 = M_{\text{shell}} / (2\mu)$ and the half-weight $\mu$ (half the average
fragment mass) from the PAFRAG-Mott formulation (Gold 2017, eq. 16) is:

$$
\mu = \sqrt{\frac{2}{\rho}}\left(\frac{\sigma_F}{\gamma}\right)^{3/2}
\left(\frac{r_{\text{bu}}}{v_{\text{bu}}}\right)^3 \quad (4)
$$

This is algebraically identical to the form $\frac{1}{2}(2\sigma_F/\rho^{1/3}\gamma)^{3/2}(r/V)^3$;
equation (4) matches the PAFRAG source notation exactly. The $V$ of Mott's
theory is the case velocity *at the instant of fracture* — Gold (2017): "the
velocity with which the shell is moving outwards" — so it is $v_{\text{bu}} = f
V_0$ of eq. (2d), not the terminal $V_0$. Up to v0.11.0 the code substituted
$V_0$ here ($f = 1$).

**Fragment shape closure (eq. 4a–4c).** The $\gamma$ in eq. (4) is *not* the
per-grade material constant: it is Gold's (2017) shape-absorbed constant
$\gamma = \alpha^{-2/3}\gamma'$ (his eq. 6), where $\gamma'$ is Mott's material
parameter (the catalogued per-grade number) and $\alpha$ carries the fragment's
aspect. Closing $\alpha$ requires the fracture spacing $x_0$ — the half-width of
the stress-released zone around a fracture (Gold 2017, eq. 2; Mott 1947, after
eq. 5), evaluated at break-up:

$$
x_0 = \sqrt{\frac{2\sigma_F}{\rho\,\gamma'}}\;\frac{r_{\text{bu}}}{v_{\text{bu}}} \quad (4a)
$$

The fragment is idealised as a parallelepiped $\bar l \times \bar x \times
t_{\text{bu}}$ (Gold 2017, eq. 4) — a **plate**, not a cube — with mean
circumferential breadth $\bar x = \kappa_x x_0$, mean axial length $\bar l =
A_{\text{eff}}\bar x$, and thickness equal to the wall *at break-up*:

$$
\alpha = \frac{\bar l\,t_{\text{bu}}}{x_0^{2}} = A_{\text{eff}}\,\kappa_x^{2}\,\frac{t_{\text{bu}}}{x_0},
\qquad \gamma = \alpha^{-2/3}\gamma' \quad (4b)
$$

where $A_{\text{eff}} = c\,A$ is the $x^2$-weighted effective aspect ratio of
eq. (4d) below, **not** the bare literature mean $A$.

$t_{\text{bu}}$ is fixed exactly by the same incompressible-wall bookkeeping as
eq. (2b), which yields the identity $t_{\text{bu}}\,r_{\text{bu}} = t\,
\tfrac{1}{2}(r_{i,0}+r_{o,0})$. It is *forced*, not chosen: the $N_0$ fragment
faces $\bar x \bar l$ must tile the **expanded** mid-surface $M_{\text{shell}}/
(\rho\,t_{\text{bu}})$, and using the as-manufactured wall $t$ with a break-up
breadth would invent ~63 % extra case mass.

Substituting (4a)–(4b) into (4) collapses to a compact equivalent form:

$$
\mu = A_{\text{eff}}\,\kappa_x^{2}\,\frac{\sigma_F\,t_{\text{bu}}}{\gamma'}
\left(\frac{r_{\text{bu}}}{v_{\text{bu}}}\right)^{2} \quad (4c)
$$

The mean-mass step behind (4c) is $2\mu = \rho\,t_0\langle A x^{2}\rangle$, so
the aspect ratio it requires is the $x^{2}$-weighted mean, whereas the
literature value $A$ is **count**-weighted. The ratio of the two is a
dimensionless moment correction $c$, applied to $A$ and to nothing else:

$$
A_{\text{eff}} = c\,A, \qquad
c = \frac{\langle A x^{2}\rangle}{\langle A\rangle\,\langle x^{2}\rangle} \quad (4d)
$$

so the closure changes the model's *scaling*, not just its magnitude: $\rho$
cancels exactly, $\mu$ is **linear** in $\gamma'^{-1}$, $r_{\text{bu}}$ and the
wall thickness $t$, and goes as $v_{\text{bu}}^{-2}$ — where the un-shaped cube
form gave $\gamma'^{-3/2}$, $r_{\text{bu}}^{3}$, $t^{0}$ and $v_{\text{bu}}^{-3}$.
Because $f$ and the steel pair enter (4c) only as $\sigma_F/(\gamma' f^{2})$,
the break-up velocity of eq. (2d) is **degenerate** with the grade: it acts
exactly like softening $\gamma' \to \gamma' f^{2}$, so $f$ cannot be identified
from fragment-size data alone (limitation L1). Note also that while $N_0 =
M_{\text{shell}}/2\mu \propto f^{2}$ exactly, the *thresholded* count $N(>m)$
does **not**: the rising $\mu$ raises the survival factor in eq. (3) and eats
back part of the change, so thresholded counts must be recomputed, never
rescaled. Setting $A_{\text{eff}} =
\kappa_x = 1$ and $t_{\text{bu}} \to x_0$ gives $\alpha = 1$, $\gamma = \gamma'$
and recovers the cube idealisation used before v0.8.0; setting $c = 1$ recovers
the single shared $A = 1.6$ used before v0.13.0.

| Symbol            | Description                                    | Unit  | Value (105 mm M1) |
| ----------------- | ---------------------------------------------- | ----- | ----------------- |
| $\rho$           | Shell steel density                            | kg/m³ | 7 850             |
| $\sigma_F$       | Dynamic flow stress at fracture                | Pa    | 800 × 10⁶         |
| $\gamma'$        | Mott statistical fragmentation parameter (material, per grade) | — | 54.5 |
| $\gamma$          | Shape-absorbed constant $\alpha^{-2/3}\gamma'$ fed to eq. (4) | — | computed |
| $A$               | Fragment length-to-breadth ratio $\bar l/\bar x$, count-weighted literature mean | — | 1.6 |
| $c$               | Aspect-ratio moment correction, eq. (4d) — **per shell** | — | 1.1024 |
| $A_{\text{eff}}$ | Effective ($x^2$-weighted) aspect ratio $c\,A$, eq. (4d) | — | 1.764 |
| $\kappa_x$       | Mean breadth in fracture spacings $\bar x/x_0$ | —     | 1.5               |
| $\alpha$          | Fragment shape factor, eq. (4b)                | —     | computed          |
| $x_0$            | Mott fracture spacing at break-up              | m     | computed          |
| $t_{\text{bu}}$  | Case wall thickness at break-up                | m     | computed          |
| $r_{\text{bu}}$  | Mean shell radius at break-up                  | m     | computed          |
| $\mu$             | Half the average fragment mass                 | kg    | computed          |

**Sourcing of $A$ and $\kappa_x$.** $\kappa_x = 1.5$ is Mott's own finding (1)
(1947): fragment circumferential lengths lie mostly in $x_0\ldots 2x_0$ with
average $1.5x_0$. Gold restates $x_0$ *itself* as the mean breadth, i.e.
silently sets $\kappa_x = 1$; Mott is the primary source and the only one who
measures the mean. $A = 1.6$ is the cross-dataset mean width:length $1{:}1.6$
of Felix et al. (2022, §2.5), corroborated by Wilson ($1{:}1.65$) and Grady
($1{:}1.5$) — the same aspect-ratio result cited under $C_{\text{shape}}$ in §4.
Full argument and checks: `updates/mott-fragment-shape-closure/derivation.md`.

**Sourcing of $c$ (v 0.13.0).** $c$ is a moment of the *joint* $(A, m)$
fragment distribution, not a material constant, so it cannot be shared across
shells: the conditional aspect mix $A\,|\,$Group that transfers between
calibers is Felix et al. (2022) Table 3 (Grady's 155 mm HE M101 photographs),
but the weights are each shell's own Mott spectrum $N(\ge m) = N_0 e^{-\sqrt{m/\mu}}$
— and since $\mu = c\,\mu_0$, $c$ is solved per shell as the fixed point
$c = c(c\,\mu_0)$. It therefore falls with caliber and passes through 1 near
75 mm, where most of the population sits in one aspect Group and the AM–HM
floor $1/(\langle A\rangle\langle 1/A\rangle)$ takes over from the
between-Group covariance. The shipped values are
`arty.fragmentation.MOTT_ASPECT_MOMENT_C`, printed per shell in §Parameters;
each registry entry carries the product as its `aspect_ratio` field, so
$A \to A_{\text{eff}}$ is the only code change ($\mu \propto A$ exactly,
$N_0 \propto 1/(cA)$). Method band $\pm 0.6$–$3.6\%$ against a $\pm 15\%$
fidelity target; the two open assumptions behind it are limitations 16 and 17.
Derivation and checks: `updates/mass-dependent-fragment-shape/derivation.md`
§3.3b/§7.

**Note on $\gamma'$ and $\sigma_F$:** These are the dominant uncertainties.
Mott (1947 §3) *prints* γ = 53 for 0.25%C steel and γ = 67 for 0.45%C steel
(the row spacing is non-uniform: 0 / 0.1 / 0.25 / 0.45 %C), but the 0.45%C row
is the one row of the four that its own closure
γ ~ 160 P₂/(P_F(1+s_F)) fails to reproduce (−16.5 %; the other three close to
≤ 3.2 %). The shipped γ′ is therefore read off the **closure-recomputed**
column, not the printed one.
The 105 mm M1 bill of material names the body steel **WD-X1335** (spec 57-107),
taken as an AISI 1335 analog at 0.33–0.38 %C; γ′ = 54.5 is a local-linear
interpolation of the recomputed column at that band's 0.355 %C midpoint (band
spread 54.1–54.9), *not* a fit to fragment-count data. It supersedes the earlier
bracket-anchored γ = 65 (which sat just under the indicted printed 0.45%C row),
and the still earlier uncited "SAE 1045, ≈ 0.45%C" attribution. Both catalogued
grades are now interpolated on this one rule and one column
(`updates/wdss1-steel-grade/derivation.md` §9.1). Dynamic flow stress at high strain rate is typically
800–1 000 MPa for hardened steel, higher than the quasi-static value of 600 MPa.
The sensitivity section explores both.

Only the **ratio** $\sigma_F/\gamma'$ is observable: (4c) contains the pair
nowhere else, so $(k\sigma_F, k\gamma')$ reproduces $\mu$ and $N_0$ exactly for
any $k$. The split into two numbers is a reporting convention, which is why the
second catalogued grade (§*Steel-grade catalog*) moves $\gamma'$ alone. The
shape closure preserves this: $\alpha$ depends on $\sigma_F$ and $\gamma'$ only
through $x_0 \propto \sqrt{\sigma_F/\gamma'}$.

The most probable fragment mass (mode of the number-weighted PDF) is $m_{\text{mode}} = \mu/4$.

### 4 · Drag: Velocity Decay Along Flat Trajectory

For a fragment of mass $m$ flying horizontally, dividing the drag equation of motion by $v$:

$$
m \frac{dv}{ds} = -\tfrac{1}{2}\,\rho_{\text{air}}\,C_D\,A_f\,v \quad (5)
$$

This integrates to exponential decay:

$$
v(s) = V_0\,e^{-\lambda s}, \qquad
\lambda(m) = \frac{\rho_{\text{air}}\,C_D\,C_{\text{shape}}}{2\,\rho^{2/3}}\,m^{-1/3} \quad (6)
$$

where the mean presented area of a tumbling irregular fragment scales as
$A_f = C_{\text{shape}}(m/\rho)^{2/3}$, so smaller fragments decelerate faster.

| Symbol              | Description                                      | Unit  | Value |
| ------------------- | ------------------------------------------------ | ----- | ----- |
| $\rho_{\text{air}}$| Air density (sea level)                         | kg/m³ | 1.225 |
| $C_D$               | Drag coefficient, tumbling fragment              | —     | 1.28  |
| $C_{\text{shape}}$ | Mean presented-area factor vs. equal-volume cube | —     | 2.089 |

**Provenance of $C_D$ and $C_{\text{shape}}$ (v0.9.0 — derived, not fitted).**
Both constants are now anchored to DoD/DDESB (1975) *Fragment and Debris
Hazards*, "Ballistic Properties". $C_D = 1.28$ is that source's recommended
constant supersonic value (its own advice is to use the plateau rather than the
full Mach curve). $C_{\text{shape}}$ is **not** a free parameter: the source
writes fragment mass as $m = k A^{3/2}$ with $k$ the measured *ballistic
density*, and equating its retardation law to eq. (6) gives the identity

$$
C_{\text{shape}} = \left(\frac{\rho_{\text{steel}}}{k}\right)^{2/3}
\quad (6a)
$$

so at the source's recommended $k = 2600$ kg/m³ (660 gr/in³, forged-steel
projectiles and fragmentation bombs) and $\rho_{\text{steel}} = 7850$ kg/m³,
$C_{\text{shape}} = 2.089$ (combined $C_D C_{\text{shape}} = 2.674$). The
identity is implemented as `c_shape_from_ballistic_density` in
`arty.fragmentation`, so $\rho_{\text{steel}}$ cancels out of (6) exactly —
fragment retardation depends on ballistic density, not steel density.

Eq. (6a) also supplies a hard *geometric floor*: mean presented area of any
convex body is $S/4$ (Cauchy), giving $C_{\text{shape}} = 1.500$ for a cube and
$1.209$ for a sphere, the minimum-area shape. The pre-v0.9.0 pair
($C_D = 0.65$, $C_{\text{shape}} = 0.90$, combined $0.585$) sat *below* that
floor — it implied $k = 25\,400$ kg/m³, a fragment 3.2× denser than steel
presenting less area than a sphere. Validation: the adopted constant reproduces
the source's own $L_1 = 247$ m/kg$^{1/3}$ to 2.4 % (an air-density convention),
and cuts the RMS log-velocity error against the 1944 Ordnance
$(m, r, v)$ tables from 0.710 to 0.092 over arrival Mach $> 0.7$
(`updates/mach-dependent-fragment-drag/derivation.md` V1–V2; re-run per column
on the corrected tables the RMS is 0.755 → 0.096 on casualties and
0.679 → 0.098 on perforation, passing the ≤ 0.10 bar on each criterion
separately rather than on a mixture — `rebaseline-verdict.md` C7).

A Mach-dependent $C_D(M)$ was tested against the same data and **rejected**,
but *not* because it fits worse — it fits better, by ~20–25% RMS once both laws
are given the same scale freedom. It is rejected because both land inside the
±10% arrival-velocity bar over the lethal-relevant band (constant 7.1%,
Mach-dependent 5.3%), making the difference immaterial at the stated fidelity
target, while adopting it would replace the closed form with a per-fragment ODE
march. The earlier "does not beat the constant (RMS 0.072 vs 0.047)" reading
published here was computed from a superseded Figure-3 digitization and a
mixed-column velocity set, and is **withdrawn** (`rebaseline-verdict.md` C11).
Residual limitations: #7, and #15 for the speed-dependence the constant does
not represent.

### 5 · Kinetic Energy and Fragmentation Field

Kinetic energy at distance $s$ from burst:

$$
E_k(s,m) = \tfrac{1}{2}\,m\,V_0^2\,e^{-2\lambda(m)\,s} \quad (7)
$$

The Mott number-density PDF (fragments per unit mass interval):

$$
n(m) = \frac{N_0}{2\sqrt{\mu\,m}}\,\exp\!\left(-\sqrt{m/\mu}\right) \quad (8)
$$

The ES-310 lethality curve $P_{k|\text{hit}}(E)$ is a log-linear interpolation between
three anchors — 100 J → 0.10, 1 kJ → 0.50, 4 kJ → 0.90 — clipped to $[0,\,0.90]$.

Expected lethal hits on a target of presented width $w$ at distance $r$
(disk geometry, azimuthally uniform spray):

$$
N_{\text{eff}}(r) = \int_0^\infty n(m)\;P_{k|\text{hit}}\!\left(E_k(r,m)\right)\frac{w}{2\pi r}\,dm \quad (9)
$$

Kill probability (Poisson, single target):

$$
P_{\text{kill}}(r) = 1 - \exp\!\left(-N_{\text{eff}}(r)\right) \quad (10)
$$

$R_{50}$ is the distance at which $P_{\text{kill}} = 0.5$.

### 6 · Burst Geometry and Height of Burst

Equations (1)–(10) describe the fragment field as a function of *slant range*
$s$ from the burst point, with no reference to where the burst sits relative
to the ground or where the fragments land. The disk geometry of eq. (9)
implicitly assumes an azimuthally uniform spray intersecting a vertical
target at the same height as the burst. Real artillery bursts occur at a
finite **height of burst** $h_b$, and the shell arrives along a sloped
trajectory. Both effects break the disk symmetry and govern how the
fragment field is mapped onto the ground. The equations below are the
foundation for the four-zone ground projection (§6.5, eq. 13–14), where
the implementation lives in `arty.zones`.

(Equation numbers (11)–(14) are reserved by the four-zone section; the new
relations introduced here are numbered from (15).)

#### Slant range and arrival elevation

For a burst at height $h_b$ above flat ground, a ground patch at horizontal
offset $(x_g, y_g)$ from the burst's ground track lies at slant range

$$
s = \sqrt{x_g^2 + y_g^2 + h_b^2} \quad (15)
$$

A fragment reaching that patch travelled along the burst-to-patch line, so
it arrives at an **elevation angle** $\gamma$ below the horizontal given by

$$
\sin\gamma = \frac{h_b}{s} \quad (16)
$$

Directly under the burst ($x_g = y_g = 0$) the arrival is vertical
($\gamma = 90°$); far out on the ground ($\sqrt{x_g^2+y_g^2}\gg h_b$) the
arrival grazes the surface ($\gamma \to 0$). This $\gamma$ is exactly the
arrival angle fed to the presented-area model $A_p(\gamma,\text{posture})$
(§6.6).

| Symbol           | Description                                   | Unit |
| ---------------- | --------------------------------------------- | ---- |
| $h_b$            | Height of burst above ground                  | m    |
| $(x_g, y_g)$     | Ground-patch offset from burst ground track   | m    |
| $s$              | Slant range, burst point to ground patch      | m    |
| $\gamma$         | Fragment arrival elevation angle below horizontal | rad/° |

#### Ground footprint scaling

A fragment leaving the burst point $(0,0,h_b)$ along unit velocity
$(\hat v_{g,x}, \hat v_{g,y}, \hat v_{g,z})$ with downward component
$\hat v_{g,z} < 0$ strikes the ground at

$$
x_\text{hit} = -\frac{\hat v_{g,x}}{\hat v_{g,z}}\,h_b, \qquad
y_\text{hit} = -\frac{\hat v_{g,y}}{\hat v_{g,z}}\,h_b \quad (= \text{eq. }14)
$$

(this is eq. 14 of §6.5, restated; the direction cosines come from the AoF
rotation, eq. 13a–c). Because $h_b$ multiplies both coordinates, the entire
ground footprint **scales linearly with burst height**: doubling $h_b$
doubles every hit distance and quadruples the footprint area, while leaving
the angular structure of the spray untouched. Height of burst is therefore
the single knob that trades footprint *size* against fragment *density* and
arrival *angle*.

#### Ground burst versus airburst

At $h_b = 0$ (contact burst) eq. (14) collapses: every fragment with a
downward component hits within a few metres of the impact point. Lethality
is intense but the lethal area is tiny — much of the spray is wasted into
the ground or over the heads of nearby targets. As $h_b$ increases the
footprint expands (linearly, above) and the *average* arrival angle
$\gamma$ falls: fragments reach a given ground patch more obliquely.

The arrival angle controls how much of the target a fragment "sees". For a
standing target the presented silhouette combines a frontal term that
scales with $\cos\gamma$ and an overhead term that scales with $\sin\gamma$:
schematically $A_p \sim A_f\cos\gamma + A_t\sin\gamma$, with $A_f$ the
frontal and $A_t$ the plan (overhead) silhouette. A steep overhead burst
($\gamma\to 90°$) presents only the small plan area $A_t$ — the standing
target is well protected; a grazing arrival ($\gamma\to 0$) presents the
full frontal area $A_f$ — the target is maximally exposed. This is the
mechanism encoded in `presented_area(γ, posture)` in `arty.fragmentation`
(§6.6, eq. 22′), and it is why optimal HOB is a compromise: high enough to
spread the footprint and lower $\gamma$ onto standing targets, low enough
that density has not thinned below the lethal threshold.

#### Angle of fall (AoF)

The shell arrives along its trajectory at **angle of fall** AoF measured
from horizontal: AoF $= 0°$ is a horizontal trajectory, AoF $= 90°$ a
vertical plunge. AoF tilts the entire spray cone via the rotation
$R_y(\text{AoF})$ (eq. 13a–c), breaking the azimuthal symmetry that eq. (9)
assumes. Two limits make the effect concrete:

- **AoF $= 0°$ (flat trajectory).** The equatorial (cylinder) spray forms a
  vertical ring around the burst. Fragments going exactly sideways are
  horizontal and never reach the ground; the downward-going half of the ring
  does land, but projects to a transverse strip at $x = 0$ directly below the
  burst — not a forward footprint. The extended forward and rearward ground
  coverage comes from the ogive and base/boattail zones, whose spray cones
  are tilted fore and aft of the equatorial plane.
- **AoF $= 90°$ (vertical plunge).** The spray is azimuthally symmetric
  about the vertical. Each zone's cone projects to a clean ring; a zone
  with spray half-angle $\theta^z$ from the (now downward) shell axis
  strikes a ring of radius

$$
r_\text{ring} = h_b\,\tan\theta^z \quad (17)
$$

  Per-zone angles $\theta^z$ are defined in §6.1; the ogive ring
  spot-check in §6.5 verifies eq. (17) numerically.

For realistic indirect fire the AoF is intermediate. WW2 105 mm howitzer
fire at 4–6 km range falls at AoF $\approx 20°$–$35°$, so the spray cone is
only modestly tilted: the forward sector of the footprint receives
substantially more fragment density than the rear. The **1-D symmetric disk**
of eq. (9) deliberately averages over that azimuthal structure, giving a
**conservative** (rear-biased, density-averaged) reading; the **four-zone 3-D
field** (§6.7) resolves the fore/aft lobes instead. The two are kept side by
side, not one superseding the other — see the three-variant division of labor
in §6.

| Symbol               | Description                                      | Unit |
| -------------------- | ------------------------------------------------ | ---- |
| AoF                  | Angle of fall, trajectory below horizontal (0°=flat, 90°=plunge) | ° |
| $(x_\text{hit}, y_\text{hit})$ | Ground-impact coordinates of a fragment | m    |
| $\theta^z$           | Per-zone spray half-angle from shell axis (§6.1) | °    |
| $r_\text{ring}$      | Ground ring radius for symmetric (AoF = 90°) burst | m  |
